Extract the stated contributions of "Anchor extremity and proportional anchor influence: A preregistered, model-based test in open trial-level data".

**Abstract**:
<paper_abstract>
Anchors bias numeric estimates, but it is unclear whether an anchor’s proportional influence rises, stays constant or falls as the anchor becomes more extreme. Meta-analyses report larger standardised effects for more distant anchors, yet a standardised mean difference rises with anchor distance even when the proportional pull is constant. We derived the shape of the anchor-response function from five process models, simulated them on the designs of the Open Anchoring Quest, and preregistered the predictions before reading any estimates. In 20 item-study cells with at least three anchor values (7,949 estimates; 83% from one study with random anchors for lengths and heights), the log-scale elasticity of estimates with respect to anchors averaged 0.31 and fell as anchors moved away from the true value (curvature -0.041, 95% CI [-0.058, -0.023]). This contradicts anchor-and-adjust with a fixed number of adjustments and constant-weight integration on the log scale, and matches the direction predicted by plausibility-based models, which however predicted a steeper decline. Across 128 two-anchor cells from 40 studies with researcher-chosen anchors, the anchoring index did not change detectably with extremity (slope 0.050, [-0.013, 0.113]). No model reproduced both patterns; a resource-rational variant passed the preregistered checks only because its predictions were very wide. Within items, extreme anchors pull estimates by a smaller share of their distance, at least for random anchors; whether this holds for deliberately chosen anchors remains open.

**Keywords**: anchoring, anchor extremity, process models, resource rationality, secondary data analysis, preregistration
</paper_abstract>

**Introduction**:
<paper_intro>
Numeric judgements are drawn towards numbers people have just considered. In the classic demonstration, participants who first judged whether the percentage of African countries in the United Nations was higher or lower than a random number gave estimates that moved towards that number (Tversky & Kahneman, 1974). The effect appears with arbitrary and informative anchors, with lay people and experts, and in consequential settings such as property valuation and criminal sentencing (Englich et al., 2006; Furnham & Boo, 2011; Northcraft & Neale, 1987). A meta-analysis of openly shared trial-level data from 90 anchoring studies estimated a pooled standardised effect of $g = 0.69$ (Röseler et al., 2022; Röseler & Schütz, 2022).

Whether an anchor’s influence depends on how extreme it is has practical and theoretical weight. Practically, negotiators, litigants and survey designers choose anchor values, and whether a more extreme value buys proportionally more influence than a moderate one depends on this relation. Theoretically, the leading accounts of anchoring make different predictions about this question,

<!-- PAGE BREAK -->

so the shape of the relation between anchor extremity and anchor influence is one of the few places where they can be tested against each other.
</paper_intro>

**Conclusion**:
<paper_conclusion>
Within the same questions, extreme anchors pulled estimates by a smaller share of their distance than moderate anchors. The evidence comes mostly from random anchors for lengths and heights in one study, with the same pattern in the one fixed-anchor item that had many anchor levels. It contradicts anchor-and-adjust with a fixed number of steps and constant-weight integration, and supports accounts in which an anchor's influence is limited by its plausibility, although the decline was weaker than simple plausibility models predict. Across studies with researcher-chosen anchors, the pattern was not visible. Whether deliberately chosen, informative anchors, such as opening offers in negotiations, also show diminishing returns to extremity cannot be answered with these data. The extremity function should be estimated within items, with proportional measures and with anchors of the kind used in practice.
</paper_conclusion>

Report what the paper claims. Do not evaluate the claims.

# About me

I am Lukas, a social psychologist, meta-scientist and open science advocate, who mostly uses you to get research done and build the tooling that supports it (in addition to teaching support). I have a solid understanding of software development and infrastructure, but am no expert, so that I will often need clear recommendations and explanations. Most of what I build is tooling for one-off projects, most is not intended to be production-ready or backwards-compatible. Feel free to clarify that project-by-project, but generally lean, efficient and clear code is more important than any backwards-compatible shim or edge-case handling.

I also regularly need your help in writing. For that, and in code, the most annoying failure mode is when history leaks in - when a text argues against its previous versions, or code comments are more about what is gone than about what the curent code does. Here, writing and reviewing outputs from the perspective of a new reader is essential.

# How to work

## Delegation: Fable as Orchestrator

When the session model is Fable, work **orchestrator-first**: plan, delegate substantive work to cheaper subagents, then review and synthesize. Fable itself keeps task decomposition, design decisions and judgment calls, reviewing subagent output, final synthesis and user-facing writing, plus edits so trivial that delegating would take longer. Everything else — implementation, broad searches, analyses, mechanical batch work — goes to subagents by default.

## Using sub-agents

- **Default subagent model: Opus** (`model: "opus"` on the Agent tool / workflow `agent()` calls). Drop to Sonnet or Haiku for clearly mechanical, high-volume steps; reserve Fable-model subagents for only the hardest verify/judge stages.
- **codex CLI** — via the `codex-delegate` skill: (a) independent second opinions and code review (read-only), and (b) self-contained implementation tasks with `--approve-for-me` — good for parallel, independent work streams.
- **agy CLI** (Antigravity; Gemini 3.x + others, `agy models` lists them) — via the `agy-delegate` skill: (a) **large-context reads** — digesting big files, PDFs, logs, or datasets that would bloat Claude context — and (b) **cross-model second opinions**.
- **In Workflow scripts**, reach codex/agy through cheap relay agents: `agent(relayPrompt, {model: 'sonnet', effort: 'low'})`, where `relayPrompt` says "You are a relay agent. Pass the following payload prompt through the `codex-delegate` [or `agy-delegate`] skill, wait for its answer, and return its answer verbatim as your final message; do not answer the payload yourself." followed by the payload, the working directory, and mode/model choices. The relay is pure transport — the skill holds the CLI recipe; keep payload prompts self-contained. Make sure the agents run the request in the foreground, with generous timeout as a subagent that backgrounds codex and waits on monitors/notifications often never gets resumed, stranding the finished answer on disk. If a codex-relay subagent goes quiet, don't wait for it — `ls` for the output file and read it directly.
- Delegation must not degrade quality: give subagents complete, self-contained prompts with all needed context and file paths, and verify load-bearing results yourself rather than trusting a subagent's summary.
- Assign clear ownership of every delegated write target. When two or more agents or processes may write the same file, branch, key, or state object at the same time, give each an independent write target. Different fields in one state file are still one shared target. Merge outputs only when reading or reporting them. If one shared target is required, use one writer, a lock, or sequential phases. Scratch files count as write targets: parallel subagents share one scratchpad directory, so tell each to name its temporary scripts and data after its own task (`scratch_refs_3.py`, not `scratch_build.py`) — otherwise one agent overwrites and executes another's file mid-run.

## Build the Small Tool

When work includes repeated edits, data processing, an analysis, a migration, or a non-trivial check, build the smallest tool that does or verifies it. Use a script, query, generator, codemod, or skill as appropriate. The tool is a reviewable artifact that someone can read and rerun.

Work through one unit to establish the recipe. Build the tool. Run it on that unit and compare its result with the hand-produced result.

Use one deterministic pass when it can handle all units. Delegate building or reviewing that tool when needed; do not assign agents to hand-apply each unit. For delegated work, put the recipe, verification steps, and files agents must not edit in one skill outside their write scope.

Commit the tool when future work will need it.

## Codex CLI (second-opinion / review)

When invoking `codex` non-interactively (e.g. for a second opinion or code review), follow this exact recipe:

1. **Feed the prompt via stdin, with `-` as the prompt arg:**
   `codex exec --skip-git-repo-check --sandbox read-only - < prompt.txt > out.txt 2>&1`
   (If you must pass the prompt as an arg, add `< /dev/null`.)
2. **Flags:** `--skip-git-repo-check` outside a git repo (codex otherwise refuses); `--sandbox read-only` for reviews/critiques; `--approve-for-me` (auto-approval inside the workspace-write sandbox), or `--dangerously-bypass-approvals-and-sandbox` to drop the sandbox, only when codex must edit files; `-m <model>` to pin a model.
3. **Run it in the background** (it can take several minutes) and write output to a file. If you need to wait, use the Monitor tool.
4. **The answer is at the END of the file.** Codex streams all its tool exploration (file reads, greps) to stdout, so the output can be thousands of lines of noise with the real prose answer last. `grep`/tail for the final section (e.g. the last `codex` / `tokens used` block) — do NOT read from the top.
5. **Unique filenames per run.** With concurrent codex runs, generic names (`prompt.txt`, `out.txt`) collide and one run can return another's answer. Always suffix by topic: `codex_prompt_<topic>.txt` / `codex_out_<topic>.txt`.

## Waiting for Background Work

Start anything expected to exceed ~90 s — R scripts, Quarto renders, test suites,
model sweeps, uploads — with `run_in_background: true` and a log file from the FIRST
attempt, not after a foreground timeout. A command killed at the 120 s default
mid-loop leaves unknown partial state, and re-running it in the foreground with a
longer timeout repeats all the work.

Pass `run_in_background: true` on its own: no `nohup`, no trailing `&`. The wrapper
returns instantly, the harness treats the run as finished, and the real process is
killed part-way — which reads as a crash in the tool you launched (a truncated log,
a zero-byte output file), not as a mistake in how it was started.

Never wait in the foreground: no `sleep N; check`, no `until ! ps -p PID` loops, no
`for i in $(seq …); do …status…; sleep; done`. Use Monitor with an until-condition
(load its schema via ToolSearch first — it is deferred). For GitHub Actions, one
backgrounded `gh run watch <id> --exit-status` replaces a polling loop.

## Using tools

- Never search from `/`; scope `find` to a directory with `-maxdepth`.
- Absolute paths in every Bash call: cwd does not persist between calls, and
  worktree checkouts (`.claude/worktrees/<branch>/`) make repo-relative paths
  resolve against the wrong base. If a path fails, `ls` its parent before retrying.
- Never resubmit a failed Edit `old_string` unchanged — re-read the exact lines
  first. Copy long prose/unicode blocks from a fresh Read, never reconstruct.
- Edit source files with the Edit tool, not Python heredocs doing string
  replacement — heredoc rewrites hide the diff.
- Reads/writes under `~/Library/CloudStorage/OneDrive-…` can ETIMEDOUT when the
  file isn't cached locally; retry once before treating as an error.  

## zsh gotchas

- `git show $ref:$path` silently mangles the argument in zsh (`:s`, `:h` and friends are parameter
modifiers) and hands git only the rev — which dumps the entire commit instead of the file, with
exit code 0. Always brace and quote: `git show "${ref}:${path}"`. Suspect this whenever a
"recovered" file is implausibly large.
- **A word starting with `=` triggers command-path expansion.** `echo ===` fails with
  `== not found` and aborts the rest of the compound command. Use `echo "---"` or
  quote it.
- **An unmatched glob is fatal, not literal.** `ls foo*`, `git branch --list bak*`,
  and `grep --include=*.html` abort with `no matches found` when nothing matches.
  Quote globs passed as arguments (`--include='*.html'`); guard optional ones
  (`ls foo* 2>/dev/null || true`).

## Chrome Extension: Local Files, Tabs, Busy Pages

- The extension cannot open `file://` URLs. To view local HTML, serve the directory
  (`python3 -m http.server <port>`, backgrounded) and open
  `http://localhost:<port>/<file>`.
- Never reuse a tabId from an earlier turn or session; call tabs_context_mcp for
  live IDs after any tab error. Don't make navigate the first action of a
  browser_batch — create the tab first.
- If a screenshot/scroll/javascript call times out, the page is mid-load: take one
  screenshot to see the state instead of reissuing the identical call. Never put
  `await new Promise(r => setTimeout(…))` inside injected JS — the CDP call itself
  then times out.

## Google Workspace

For any Google Workspace task (Docs, Sheets, Drive, Gmail, Calendar, Slides, Forms), use the `gws` CLI (`/opt/homebrew/bin/gws`). Discover the API with `gws <service> --help` and `gws schema <service.resource.method>`. Fall back to browser automation only for things gws cannot do, such as viewing rendered output.

Never pipe `gws` output directly into a JSON parser: keyring warnings and preamble
contaminate stdout. Write to a file first (`gws … --format json > out.json 2>err.log`),
`head -c 300` it to confirm it is JSON, then parse. Pass API arguments through
`--params '<JSON>'`, not as flags or positionals. After parsing any API response,
print the top-level keys before indexing into them.

## Sanity-Check Prompts

If a user prompt seems unrelated to the current project/working directory, or references files, concepts, or protocols that don't exist in the codebase, ask the user to confirm before proceeding. They may be in the wrong folder.

## Scratch / Throwaway Files

Name temporary or throwaway files with a `scratch` prefix (e.g. `scratch.py`, `scratch_notes.md`, `scratch_test.js`). The `/wrap` end-of-session skill detects files matching `scratch*` and offers to commit or delete them during wrap-up.

## Recurring Corrections Become Mechanisms

When the same correction or unexpected failure recurs, encode the fix in a mechanism: a test, hook, lint rule, validation step, safer code default, or automation. Apply the mechanism now and remove the duplicate prose.

Use the strongest mechanism available. Prefer a restriction that makes an invalid state impossible. If that is not possible, use a lint or CI check, a shared helper, or a runtime check.

Keep a prose rule only when it requires judgment. State the decision and the failure mode it prevents.

## Statistical analyses

In my research, I often need your help with statistical analyses. Make sure these are appropriate and robust. If we change direction and another analysis approach becomes more appropriate, we should generally change track (unless compute cost is very high).

### Reproducing / Replicating Prior Analyses

When reproducing, replicating, or re-analysing a previous study, match the original as faithfully as possible by DEFAULT — same sample inclusion rules, same variables, same operationalisations, same model. Do NOT introduce deviations (different year ranges, team/group-size filters, measures, controls, transformations) for convenience, tractability, or unstated preference. If a deviation is genuinely warranted (e.g. to fix a confound, handle censoring, or reduce compute), STOP and flag it explicitly, explain why, and get agreement before building on it. When a deviation is kept, state it and its justification plainly in the writeup and flag it briefly in the code.

# Writing

## Status Reports and Summaries: Plain Over Clever

When reporting progress, findings, or decisions, write like a technical changelog,
not a narrated story. The test: could someone who did not watch the work act on
each sentence without rereading it or asking what it refers to? For that, largely use
ASD-STE100, but deviate where that increases clarity and readability.

Concretely:

1. **Lead with the fact, not the framing.** "Added a manifest hash check at Stage 3
   startup; hashing 300 MB takes 0.10 s" — not "The manifest binding is in,
   positioned with the other startup refusals, and the agent measured the cost
   rather than assuming it."
2. **No process narration.** Skip who suggested what, what was declined, what an
   agent "pushed back" on, and why a fix is "worth noting". Report the decision and
   its one-line reason; drop the story of how it was reached unless asked.
3. **Resolve every reference in place.** Never write "#17", "the #8 question",
   or a label coined earlier in the session without saying what
   it is: "finding #17 (rule-pick caching during outages)". Assume the reader has
   no memory of the earlier conversation.
4. **One clause, one fact.** No sentences that stack a claim, its justification,
   and a contrast with an alternative separated by dashes. Split them.
5. **Structure over prose for multi-item status.** Three or more parallel items
   (fixes applied, decisions pending, open questions) go in a list or short table
   with a bolded label per item, not woven into paragraphs.
6. **Ban editorializing connectors**: "which is the entire point", "worth noting
   because", "the honest answer is", "notably". State the fact; let it carry its
   own weight.
7. **Separate done / pending / needs-my-decision** into visibly distinct blocks,
   so nothing waiting on the user is buried mid-paragraph.

## Jargon: I Know the Concepts, Not the Vocabulary

I have a solid working understanding of programming and systems, but no formal CS
training. Do not dumb things down or pad explanations — just prefer the plain term
when one exists and carries the same meaning: "check before writing" over
"TOCTOU-safe", "lookup table" over "hashmap semantics", "partly overwritten file" 
over "torn write". When a term of art is genuinely the precise word (idempotent, race condition), 
use it, and add a five-word gloss in parentheses the first time it appears in a session if the
meaning isn't clear from context. Never use jargon as compression when a plain
phrase is barely longer.

## Style Guides

My written style guides live in `~/Documents/Coding/style_guides`:

- `academic/wallrich_academic_style_guide.md` — voice, spelling, hedging, banned vocabulary, sentence structure, citations, footnotes. Section-specific detail in `academic/sections/{introduction,methods,discussion}.md`. 
- `teaching/wallrich_teaching_style_guide.md` — slides, workshops, handouts, and other audience-facing material.

Read the relevant guide before drafting, revising, or reviewing my prose in that register, and before proposing additions to it.

## Statistical Results in Quarto/Rmd Reports

CRITICAL: NEVER write interpretive prose about statistical results you haven't seen. Produce the numbers first, read the rendered output, then write the text. The full conventions are in the `quarto-reporting` skill. Load it when creating or editing `.qmd` or `.Rmd` files.

## Academic References and DOIs

CRITICAL: NEVER fabricate DOIs, citation metadata, or reference details from memory. DOIs, author lists, titles, page numbers, and volume/issue numbers are exact identifiers — getting them wrong is worse than omitting them.

When creating references:
1. **Always look up DOIs** via the Crossref API (`https://api.crossref.org/works?query.bibliographic={url_encoded_reference}`) or web search. Never guess a DOI.
2. **Verify each DOI resolves** by fetching `https://api.crossref.org/works/{DOI}` and checking the returned metadata matches.
3. If a DOI cannot be found, **omit the DOI field** rather than inventing one.
4. For author names, titles, and publication details: verify against Crossref metadata or the publisher's website. Do not rely on memory for these details.

## Reading Academic Articles from HTML

When reading an academic article from an HTML page, ensure the page has fully loaded before extracting or searching its text, and confirm you are actually looking at the full text rather than just the abstract/landing view. A search that comes back empty can mean the content hasn't rendered yet, not that it isn't there. Take a screenshot to see what is actually on the page, before concluding a section is missing or treating the abstract as the whole article.

## Key failure mode - insufficient editing / drift

### The text has no memory of its drafts

Readers see only the final text, never its revision history. They do not know what an earlier draft said, what was wrong with it, or why a claim was softened or dropped. All external writing must read as a clean, self-contained statement of the *current* message, not as a reply to a previous version. Watch for "history leakage": phrasing that only makes sense against a framing the reader never saw. Tells include "not simply X", "rather than Y", "this is not the wrong variable", "to be fair", "the honest limits are narrower", "less a reprieve than a reminder", "we no longer…", and defensive hedges that rebut objections raised only in our own discussion. State the positive claim directly — say what the thing IS and what genuinely limits it, not what it is not relative to a draft.

This applies with full force to durable reference text: CLAUDE.md rules, code comments, docs, commit messages, skill files. A rule states the current fact ("GNU coreutils is on PATH"), never the story of its own correction — no "installed Jul 2026", "exists now", "no longer missing", "fixed since", "never assume X is absent". Those phrasings only make sense to someone who held the old, wrong belief; every future reader starts from the rule itself. Before saving any rule or comment, reread it as a stranger: if it reads as a rebuttal, rewrite it as the fact.

### When we agree to restructure, actually restart

If you and I agree to write a *fresh* draft or a new outline rather than edit the existing one, write it fresh from the agreed outline. Do not silently carry over the previous version's spine, ordering, emphasis, or lead just because it's already there — that is how an obsolete framing survives a "rewrite." Carry over only the verified facts, numbers and sources; treat the prior draft's structure as superseded unless we explicitly decide to keep a part of it.

# HTML files as a common output

Whenever you write long plans, proposals or report, assume HTML output as a default. It is more readable than md. When you need detailed feedback, include */html-comments*.

Link identifiers wherever they resolve: DOIs as `https://doi.org/…`, arXiv IDs as `https://arxiv.org/abs/…`, repos, issues, dataset accessions. Cited constructs (a named statistic, rubric or method) get a short hover gloss (`<abbr title="…">`) and a References section at the end.

- Always include a short description summarizing what the agent will do
- When the agent is done, its final report is not visible to the user. To show the user the result, you should send a text message back to the user with a concise summary of the result.
- Trust but verify: an agent's summary describes what it intended to do, not necessarily what it did. When an agent writes or edits code, check the actual changes before reporting the work as done.
- Agents run in the background by default. When an agent runs in the background, you will be automatically notified when it completes — do NOT sleep, poll, or proactively check on its progress. Continue with other work or respond to the user instead.
- **Foreground vs background**: Pass `run_in_background: false` only when your very next action depends on the agent's result and nothing else could usefully happen while it runs — e.g., a research agent whose finding gates the edit you're about to make. Otherwise let it run in the background (the default) — this includes fire-and-forget work, independent investigations, and anything where the user might hand you something else in the meantime. Wanting the result "next" is not enough on its own.
- **Don't race**: after launching a background agent, you know nothing about its results. Never fabricate or predict them in any format — not as prose, summary, or structured output. - To continue a previously spawned agent, use SendMessage with the agent's ID or name as the `to` field — that resumes it with full context. A new Agent call starts a fresh agent with no memory of prior runs, so the prompt must be self-contained.
- Each agent type's model, reasoning effort, and tool access are set in its definition (`.claude/agents/*.md` frontmatter, or the SDK `agents` option); the `model` parameter here overrides the definition for this one call.
- Clearly tell the agent whether you expect it to write code or just to do research (search, file reads, web fetches, etc.), since a fresh agent is not aware of the user's intent

Brief the agent like a smart colleague who just walked into the room — it hasn't seen this conversation, doesn't know what you've tried, doesn't understand why this task matters.
- Explain what you're trying to accomplish and why.
- Describe what you've already learned or ruled out.
- Give enough context about the surrounding problem that the agent can make judgment calls rather than just following a narrow instruction.
- If you need a short response, say so ("report in under 200 words").

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

77	
78	**Abstract**
79	
80	Anchors bias numeric estimates, but it is unclear whether an anchor's proportional influence rises, stays constant or falls as the anchor becomes more extreme. Meta-analyses report larger standardised effects for more distant anchors, yet a standardised mean difference rises with anchor distance even when the proportional pull is constant. We derived the shape of the anchor-response function from five process models, simulated them on the designs of the Open Anchoring Quest, and preregistered the predictions before reading any estimates. In `r dc$within_cells` item-study cells with at least three anchor values (`r nf(P$n_rows)` estimates; `r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * wct[study == "Bahník, 2021a", sum(estimates)] / P$n_rows)` from one study with random anchors for lengths and heights), the log-scale elasticity of estimates with respect to anchors averaged `r f2(P$b)` and fell as anchors moved away from the true value (curvature `r f3(P$g)`, 95% CI `r ci(P$g_lo, P$g_hi)`). This contradicts anchor-and-adjust with a fixed number of adjustments and constant-weight integration on the log scale, and matches the direction predicted by plausibility-based models, which however predicted a steeper decline. Across `r h2$n_cells` two-anchor cells from `r h2$n_studies` studies with researcher-chosen anchors, the anchoring index did not change detectably with extremity (slope `r f3(h2$slope)`, `r ci(h2$slope_lo, h2$slope_hi)`). No model reproduced both patterns; a resource-rational variant passed the preregistered checks only because its predictions were very wide. Within items, estimates respond less to changes in the anchor when the anchor is far from the true value, at least for random anchors; whether this holds for deliberately chosen anchors remains open.
81	
82	**Keywords:** anchoring, anchor extremity, process models, resource rationality, secondary data analysis, preregistration
83	
84	# Introduction
85	
86	Numeric judgements are drawn towards numbers people have just considered. In the classic demonstration, participants who first judged whether the percentage of African countries in the United Nations was higher or lower than a random number gave estimates that moved towards that number [@tversky1974]. The effect appears with arbitrary and informative anchors, with lay people and experts, and in consequential settings such as property valuation and criminal sentencing [@northcraft1987; @englich2006; @furnham2011]. A meta-analysis of openly shared trial-level data from 90 anchoring studies estimated a pooled standardised effect of *g* = 0.69 [@roseler2022meta; @roseler2022opaq].
87	
88	Whether an anchor's influence depends on how extreme it is has practical and theoretical weight. Practically, negotiators, litigants and survey designers choose anchor values, and whether a more extreme value buys proportionally more influence than a moderate one depends on this relation. Theoretically, the leading accounts of anchoring make different predictions about this question, so the shape of the relation between anchor extremity and anchor influence is one of the few places where they can be tested against each other.
89	
90	## Evidence on anchor extremity
91	
92	Experiments that varied anchor extremity have produced mixed results. @chapman1994 found that "implausibly extreme anchors had a proportionally smaller effect than anchors close to the expected value" [p. 223] in lottery valuations. @strack1997 found that implausible anchors were at least as effective as plausible ones in standardised estimates. Two implausible high anchors that differed greatly (e.g., 214 and 271 years for Gandhi's age at death) produced similar estimates [@mussweiler2001], and @wegener2001 found that very extreme anchors had smaller effects than moderate ones. These studies compared two to four anchor levels, mostly for a handful of items. The most fine-grained test so far used a perceptual task: @imhoff2023 [Study 2] showed participants dot patterns of about 500 dots next to standards labelled with their exact number of dots, which differed from the target by up to 400 dots in 20-dot steps. Estimates were drawn towards these symbolic anchors, but the pull levelled off once the anchor differed from the target by more than about 300 dots.
93	
94	The two recent meta-analyses reach different conclusions. Using the Open Anchoring Quest (OpAQ) data, @roseler2022meta found that Hedges' *g* increased with the relative distance between anchor and true value and concluded against the prediction that extreme anchors produce smaller effects. @schley2026 coded extremity as a binary flag, mainly for anchors that the original authors described as extreme or implausible, and found no difference in effect size. @barrera2024 modelled the anchored crowd mean as a weighted average of anchor and crowd mean, with a weight that decays exponentially with the distance between anchor and truth, and found that this weight fell with distance across 30 percentage questions.
95	
96	These results are hard to compare because they measure anchor influence in different units. A standardised mean difference between high- and low-anchor conditions rises with the distance between the anchors even if every anchor pulls estimates by the same proportion of its distance. A finding that *g* grows with anchor distance is therefore compatible with constant, rising and falling proportional influence. The theories speak to the proportional pull: how much of the distance between belief and anchor is carried into the estimate. @jacowitz1995 captured this with the anchoring index, the difference between median estimates under high and low anchors divided by the difference between the anchors, and @roseler2022meta called for such a unitless measure "to formalize the relationship between anchor distance and adjustment strength" [@roseler2022meta, p. 34].
97	
98	## Process models and their predictions
99	
100	We consider five process models. Each maps an anchor and a belief onto an estimate, and each implies a shape for the relation between anchor extremity and proportional pull ([@fig-models]). The models are specific formal implementations, all defined on the log scale of the estimated quantity; a test of one of them is a test of that implementation, not of every version of the theory that inspired it.
101	
102	In *anchor-and-adjust with a fixed number of adjustments* (M1), people start at the anchor and adjust towards their belief in a limited number of stochastic steps. This is not a theory anyone has defended in its own right; it is the mechanistic core of the resource-rational account with the number of adjustments held constant, as in Lieder et al.'s fit to Jacowitz and Kahneman's data (29 adjustments), and it shows what adjustment alone implies. @lieder2018a formalised adjustment as a Metropolis-Hastings chain that starts at the anchor and moves towards the belief distribution. When the anchor is far away, each step covers a bounded distance, so a fixed number of steps leaves a larger share of the distance uncorrected, and the proportional pull rises with extremity. Lieder et al. approximated the chain's convergence as geometric, which implies a constant proportional pull (their Eq. 4); that approximation holds for anchors near the belief, and our simulations use the chain itself.
103	
104	In *resource-rational anchor-and-adjust* (M1R), the number of adjustments is chosen to minimise expected error plus a time cost per adjustment [@lieder2018a, Eq. 2]. Anchors inside the plausible range are barely adjusted, because adjusting from them buys little accuracy, while far anchors justify many adjustments. The resulting pull can fall with extremity, but its shape depends on the time cost and on how uncertain people are.
105	
106	In *constant-weight integration* (M2), the estimate is a weighted average of anchor and belief with a fixed weight. This is the simplest version of the anchor integration model [@turner2016], and in log units it implies a constant proportional pull. It is the null model for shape. A constant weight on the raw scale would instead imply a declining log-scale elasticity for anchors below the belief and a rising one above it; we examine this variant in an exploratory analysis.
107	
108	In *adjustment to the plausible boundary* (M3), people accept anchors that lie inside the range of values they find plausible and adjust from implausible anchors only until they reach the edge of that range [@mussweiler2001; @epley2006]. @epley2006 proposed this stopping rule for self-generated anchors; M3 applies it to provided anchors. Beyond the boundary the estimate stops moving, so the proportional pull falls towards zero.
109	
110	In *plausibility-discounted integration* (M4), the anchor's weight declines as the anchor becomes implausible. This formalises the proposal that extreme anchors lose influence because they are implausible [@wegener2001], and it resembles the anchor integration model, in which an anchor's influence depends on how consistent it is with prior beliefs [@turner2016]. Selective-accessibility accounts, in which anchoring arises from anchor-consistent knowledge activated during the comparison [@strack1997; @mussweiler1999], have been read as predicting smaller effects for implausible anchors [@roseler2022meta]. The pull falls, and far enough out, a more extreme anchor moves the estimate back towards the belief.
111	
112	```{r fig-models}
113	#| fig-alt: "Two line charts of five models against anchor distance from the belief centre. Left: mean estimate; M1 and M2 rise linearly, M1R, M3 and M4 flatten beyond about one unit. Right: local elasticity; M1 rises with distance, M2 is flat, M1R, M3 and M4 fall to zero or below."
114	#| fig-cap: "Model predictions at the median calibrated parameter values. (A) Mean log estimate relative to the belief centre as a function of the anchor's distance from the belief centre, in units of belief uncertainty. (B) Local elasticity, the proportional pull of the anchor. M1: anchor-and-adjust with a fixed number of adjustments; M1R: resource-rational anchor-and-adjust; M2: constant-weight integration; M3: adjustment to the plausible boundary; M4: plausibility-discounted integration. Figure produced with R code written by an AI system (see Method)."
115	knitr::include_graphics(here("manuscript", "figures", "fig1_model_predictions.png"))
116	```
117	
118	The models also include a no-anchoring baseline (M0). Lieder et al. derived that bias grows linearly with anchor distance when the number of adjustments is fixed, showed how the optimal number of adjustments depends on distance, and fitted a five-level anchoring demonstration in which bias rose linearly with the anchor, but did not examine whether proportional influence changes for implausibly extreme anchors. @turner2016 built an inverted U between anchor extremity and the size of the shift in estimates into their model "for simplicity" and tested it with one anchor per item.
119	
120	## The present study
121	
122	We tested these predictions on OpAQ, an openly licensed collection of trial-level anchoring data [@roseler2022opaq]. Because anchor values in most studies were chosen by the original authors together with the items, a comparison across items confounds extremity with item properties. Our primary test is therefore within items: in studies that presented many different anchors for the same question, we asked how the proportional pull changes as the anchor moves away from the true value. Compared with the dot-estimation evidence of @imhoff2023, these studies use general-knowledge magnitudes and anchors that lie up to several orders of magnitude from the true value. A comparison of the anchoring index across two-anchor studies is a secondary test. We simulated every model on the exact OpAQ designs to derive numeric predictions and passed the simulated data through the same estimators as the observed data. We preregistered the predictions, decision rules and analyses before reading any estimate.
123	
124	# Method
125	
126	## Transparency and openness
127	
128	The preregistration (following the secondary-data template of @vandenakker2021), the frozen model predictions, all code and all outputs are in the project repository. The preregistration was committed to version control before the estimates were read; a reader function refuses to load the outcome column unless the preregistration is committed. The one-command script `run_all.sh` reproduces every number from the raw data. Four deviations from the preregistration are listed in the section on deviations below. The study was designed, coded, analysed and written by an AI system under the instruction of the author, as described in the next section.
129	
130	## Use of AI tools
131	
132	The study was carried out by an AI system, Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic; model identifier claude-opus-5-5), running in Claude Code between 27 and 28 September 2026 under the instruction of the author. The instruction asked for a complete, preregistered study in judgement and decision making based on openly licensed data, with decisions recorded and reviews by other AI systems. The AI searched the literature and data repositories (with subagents of the same model), chose the research question and dataset, specified the models, wrote the preregistration and all analysis code in R, ran the analyses, produced the figures and tables, and drafted the text. OpenAI Codex CLI (version 0.155.1) and Google Gemini 3.8 Flash (accessed through the Antigravity command-line tool) reviewed the choice of study, the code and the manuscript; their comments and our responses are in the repository. The AI tools used no data other than the openly licensed OpAQ file and published literature. All numbers in this article are computed by code from the raw data, and all references were retrieved by script from Crossref or DataCite metadata and checked against the cited sources. The tools can be accessed commercially from Anthropic, OpenAI and Google. The author did not direct the choice of question, methods or interpretation.
133	
134	## Data
135	
136	OpAQ [@roseler2022opaq; @opaqosf] aggregates openly available and contributed anchoring datasets into one trial-level file with harmonised design codes. We used the newest version of the file (`opaq_70a.csv`, dated 10 February 2023), which contains `r nf(dc$opaq_rows)` estimates from `r dc$opaq_studies` studies and `r dc$opaq_items` items. It is licensed under CC-BY 4.0 and contains no personal identifiers beyond sex, age and nationality, none of which we used.
137	
138	Estimates entered the analysis if the anchor was explicitly random, fixed, or relevant to the target (self-generated and incidental anchors were excluded); the response scale was open; the quantity was a positive ratio-scale magnitude (e.g., a length, price, population or count, but not a date, temperature, percentage or preference); and anchor and true value were positive. We excluded one study whose anchors were computed from each participant's own unanchored estimates. Two sets were formed from these estimates.
139	
140	- **Within-item set** (primary): item-study cells with at least three distinct anchor values. Before exclusions, it contains `r dc$within_cells` cells from `r dc$within_studies` studies (`r nf(dc$within_rows)` estimates, `r nf(dc$within_participants)` participants). OpAQ codes 15 cells as using random anchors: 13 general-knowledge items from @bahnik2021, in which each participant compared 13 random anchors between 1 and 1,000 with 13 lengths, heights and distances, and two items from @yoon2021, in which the anchors were participants' own height or age. OpAQ codes five cells as using fixed anchors: four items with 10 high anchor levels each from unpublished data by Frech et al. (2021), contributed to OpAQ, and one item (the height of Cologne cathedral) with 20 anchor levels from a supplementary task in @imhoff2023 [Study 2], whose authors describe these anchors as random. We followed the OpAQ coding, as preregistered.
141	- **Across-cell set** (secondary): cells with fixed or relevant anchors, exactly one low and one high anchor value, a log ratio of at least 0.25 between them, and at least 10 estimates per anchor. Before exclusions, it contains `r dc$across_cells` cells from `r dc$across_studies` studies (`r nf(dc$across_rows)` estimates).
142	
143	[@tbl-cells] describes the within-item cells. OpAQ labels two of the source studies differently from their publications: "Bahník, 2021a" is @bahnik2021, and "Imhoff & Barker, 2022, Study 2" is a supplementary task in @imhoff2023.
144	
145	```{r tbl-cells}
146	#| tbl-cap: "The 20 within-item cells (after exclusions). Anchor levels are distinct anchor values; the range of x is the log ratio of anchor to true value. Anchor type follows the OpAQ codes; the anchors of the two Yoon et al. items were participants' own height or age, and Imhoff and Barker describe their anchors as random."
147	lab <- c("Bahník, 2021a" = "Bahník (2021)", "Frech et al., 2021" = "Frech et al. (2021)",
148	         "Yoon et al., 2021, Form C" = "Yoon et al. (2021)", "Imhoff & Barker, 2022, Study 2" = "Imhoff & Barker (2023)")
149	tc <- wct[, .(Study = lab[study], Item = sub("\\s*\\([^()]*\\)$", "", item),
150	              Unit = ifelse(grepl("\\([^()]*\\)$", item), sub(".*\\(([^()]*)\\)$", "\\1", item), "count"),
151	              `True value` = sapply(true_value, function(v) format(v, big.mark = ",", scientific = FALSE, trim = TRUE, drop0trailing = TRUE)),
152	              N = estimates, `Anchor levels` = anchor_levels, `Range of x` = sprintf("%.1f to %.1f", x_min, x_max),
153	              `Anchor type` = anchor_type)]
154	tc[, Item := sub("^(\\w)", "\\U\\1", Item, perl = TRUE)][Unit == "m", Unit := "metres"]
155	knitr::kable(tc)
156	```
157	
158	## Measures
159	
160	For every estimate we computed *y* = ln(estimate / true value) and *x* = ln(anchor / true value). Working on the log scale treats a doubling of a height and a doubling of a population alike and matches the roughly log-normal spread of numeric estimates. The log elasticity, the change in *y* per unit change in *x*, is a unitless proportional pull: an elasticity of .5 means that doubling the anchor multiplies the estimate by about 1.41.
161	
162	In the within-item set we modelled *y* = *a*~cell~ + *b*·*x* + *g*·*x*|*x*|. Here *b* is the fitted local elasticity at the true value (for an average cell), and the curvature *g* describes how the local elasticity, *b* + 2*g*|*x*|, changes as the anchor moves away from the true value in either direction. The local elasticity is the proportional change in the estimate per proportional change in the anchor at a given anchor value; it is not the share of the whole distance between belief and anchor that ends up in the estimate. We also report the relative curvature ρ = *g*/*b*, which does not depend on the overall strength of anchoring. In the across-cell set we computed each cell's log anchoring index, the difference between the median *y* under the high and the low anchor divided by the log ratio of the anchors, and each cell's extremity, the mean absolute log distance of its two anchors from the true value. The standard error of a median was approximated as 1.2533 × MAD / √*n*, where MAD is the median absolute deviation scaled by 1.4826 to estimate the standard deviation (the R default), and the standard error of the index as the square root of the summed squared standard errors of the two medians, divided by the log ratio of the anchors. No participant answered under both anchors of the same cell, so the two medians are independent.
163	
164	## Model predictions
165	
166	The five process models and the no-anchoring baseline were implemented on the log scale ([@fig-models]; specification in `R/models.R`). Every participant-item combination had a belief centre drawn around the true value, with item-level bias and between-person spread. Responses included response noise and a 2% share of gross errors. Model parameters are expressed in units of the item's belief uncertainty σ, which was drawn from 0.3 to 1.2 log units per item.
167	
168	To fix the models' parameters without using OpAQ outcomes, we calibrated each model to the anchoring index that @jacowitz1995 reported for anchors at the 15th and 85th percentiles of unanchored estimates (about .49), accepting parameter values that produced an index between .30 and .60. The preregistered calibration computed this index on the log scale; a raw-scale recalibration is reported as a sensitivity analysis. The number of accepted grid points per model was `r paste(sprintf("%s: %d", acc$model, acc$N), collapse = "; ")`. We then simulated each model on the exact OpAQ designs (the same anchors, true values, participants and cell sizes; `r n_rep[model == "M0"]$N` replicates for M0 and `r n_rep[model == "M1"]$N` for each other model), drawing parameters uniformly from the accepted grid points, and passed each simulated dataset through the estimators used for the observed data. [@tbl-predictions] lists the resulting predictions.
169	
170	```{r tbl-predictions}
171	#| tbl-cap: "Preregistered model predictions: medians and 95% predictive intervals across simulated replicates."
172	q <- function(v) sprintf("%.3f [%.3f, %.3f]", median(v), quantile(v, .025), quantile(v, .975))
173	tab <- pred[, .(`Elasticity at the true value b` = q(b), `Curvature g` = q(g),
174	                `Relative curvature ρ` = if (.BY$Model == "M0") "—" else q(rho),
175	                `Across-cell slope d` = q(across_slope)), by = .(Model = model)]
176	tab[, Model := c(M0 = "M0 No anchoring", M1 = "M1 Anchor-and-adjust, fixed", M1R = "M1R Anchor-and-adjust, resource-rational",
177	                 M2 = "M2 Constant weight", M3 = "M3 Plausible boundary", M4 = "M4 Plausibility discount")[Model]]
178	knitr::kable(tab)
179	```
180	
181	The predictions separate the models by shape. M1 predicts positive curvature (median *g* = `r f3(med_("M1", "g"))`), M2 zero curvature, and M3 and M4 negative curvature (`r f3(med_("M3", "g"))` and `r f3(med_("M4", "g"))`). M1R's curvature depends on its parameters, with a predictive interval spanning zero. The across-cell slope follows the same pattern.
182	
183	## Analysis plan
184	
185	**H1 (primary).** In the within-item set we fitted a linear mixed model with fixed effects for *x* and *x*|*x*|, uncorrelated random intercepts, slopes and curvatures by cell, and random intercepts by participant, using lme4 and lmerTest [@bates2015; @kuznetsova2017] in R [@rcore2026]. Confidence intervals for *b* and *g* used Satterthwaite degrees of freedom; the interval for ρ used a delta-method standard error. Estimates were removed as gross errors when their log distance from the true value exceeded both ln(1000) and the cell's largest anchor distance plus ln(10), a rule that never removes a response equal to an anchor. H1a and H1b applied the same model to the random-anchor and fixed-anchor strata.
186	
187	**Decision rules.** The shape test was interpreted only if the confidence interval for *b* lay above zero (gate G1). We then classified the curvature, in this order, as *flat* if the confidence interval for ρ lay within the equivalence bounds ±0.05, as *rising* if the interval for *g* lay above zero, as *falling* if it lay below zero, and otherwise as inconclusive. Using a 95% interval for this check amounts to an equivalence test at α = .025 [@lakens2017]; the bounds sit just below the smallest relative curvature in the 95% predictive interval of M1, M3 and M4 and far outside that of M2. Applied to the simulated replicates, this rule labelled data generated by M1 as rising in more than 99% of replicates, data from M3 and M4 as falling in more than 99%, data from M2 as flat in more than 99%, and data from M0 as failing the gate in all replicates. These operating characteristics are approximations: they use normal critical values, always the full random-effects structure, and a simplified version of gate G2.
188	
189	**H2 (secondary).** We regressed the cell-level log anchoring index on extremity in a multilevel meta-regression with random intercepts for studies and cells within studies [@viechtbauer2010], using standard errors derived from the median absolute deviation (MAD) of each condition. Gate G2 required the mean index to exceed zero; the slope *d* was classified with the same ordered rule and equivalence bounds of ±0.03.
190	
191	**H3 (model adequacy).** A model was contradicted when the observed curvature (*g* or ρ) or the across-cell slope *d* fell outside its 95% predictive interval; M0 was also contradicted if gate G1 passed. The observed level of anchoring (*b* and the mean index) was compared with each model's interval but did not decide survival, because levels inherit the calibration to Jacowitz and Kahneman's design.
192	
193	**Robustness.** We preregistered seven robustness analyses: median regression without the gross-error rule, with a participant-cluster bootstrap [@koenker1978; @quantreg]; separate slopes for near (|*x*| ≤ 1) and far anchors; H1 without @bahnik2021; H2 with the raw-scale anchoring index; H2 with design covariates; H2 without one study whose item coding may contain errors; and two alternative extremity measures.
194	
195	## Deviations from the preregistration
196	
197	We made four changes after the confirmatory analysis had been run. First, a code review found that the observed mean anchoring index in the H3 level check was computed with a different estimator from the simulated one; we replaced it with the same inverse-variance weighted mean. This affects only level criteria, which do not decide model survival. Second, the preregistration described one M1R parameter incorrectly; the code, and therefore the predictions, were correct. Third, we made code changes that altered no reported number, and we disclose two numerical safeguards that were in the preregistered code but not in its text (a floor for the MAD and the exclusion of cells with zero standard error in one robustness analysis); neither affected the analysed data. Fourth, we clarified that the relative-curvature interval uses a normal critical value. One cell (Shanks et al., 2020, Study 3, the population of Chicago) was excluded in full: its participants answered in millions, while its anchors and true value were raw counts, so all of its responses exceeded the preregistered gross-error limit. All analyses labelled exploratory or sensitivity were added after the preregistration.
198

**Abstract**

Anchors bias numeric estimates, but it is unclear whether an anchor's proportional influence rises, stays constant or falls as the anchor becomes more extreme. Meta-analyses report larger standardised effects for more distant anchors, yet a standardised mean difference rises with anchor distance even when the proportional pull is constant. We derived the shape of the anchor-response function from five process models, simulated them on the designs of the Open Anchoring Quest, and preregistered the predictions before reading any estimates. In `r dc$within_cells` item-study cells with at least three anchor values (`r nf(P$n_rows)` estimates; `r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * wct[study == "Bahník, 2021a", sum(estimates)] / P$n_rows)` from one study with random anchors for lengths and heights), the log-scale elasticity of estimates with respect to anchors averaged `r f2(P$b)` and fell as anchors moved away from the true value (curvature `r f3(P$g)`, 95% CI `r ci(P$g_lo, P$g_hi)`). This contradicts anchor-and-adjust with a fixed number of adjustments and constant-weight integration on the log scale, and matches the direction predicted by plausibility-based models, which however predicted a steeper decline. Across `r h2$n_cells` two-anchor cells from `r h2$n_studies` studies with researcher-chosen anchors, the anchoring index did not change detectably with extremity (slope `r f3(h2$slope)`, `r ci(h2$slope_lo, h2$slope_hi)`). No model reproduced both patterns; a resource-rational variant passed the preregistered checks only because its predictions were very wide. Within items, estimates respond less to changes in the anchor when the anchor is far from the true value, at least for random anchors; whether this holds for deliberately chosen anchors remains open.

# Introduction

Numeric judgements are drawn towards numbers people have just considered. In the classic demonstration, participants who first judged whether the percentage of African countries in the United Nations was higher or lower than a random number gave estimates that moved towards that number [@tversky1974]. The effect appears with arbitrary and informative anchors, with lay people and experts, and in consequential settings such as property valuation and criminal sentencing [@northcraft1987; @englich2006; @furnham2011]. A meta-analysis of openly shared trial-level data from 90 anchoring studies estimated a pooled standardised effect of *g* = 0.69 [@roseler2022meta; @roseler2022opaq].

Whether an anchor's influence depends on how extreme it is has practical and theoretical weight. Practically, negotiators, litigants and survey designers choose anchor values, and whether a more extreme value buys proportionally more influence than a moderate one depends on this relation. Theoretically, the leading accounts of anchoring make different predictions about this question, so the shape of the relation between anchor extremity and anchor influence is one of the few places where they can be tested against each other.

## Evidence on anchor extremity

Experiments that varied anchor extremity have produced mixed results. @chapman1994 found that "implausibly extreme anchors had a proportionally smaller effect than anchors close to the expected value" [p. 223] in lottery valuations. @strack1997 found that implausible anchors were at least as effective as plausible ones in standardised estimates. Two implausible high anchors that differed greatly (e.g., 214 and 271 years for Gandhi's age at death) produced similar estimates [@mussweiler2001], and @wegener2001 found that very extreme anchors had smaller effects than moderate ones. These studies compared two to four anchor levels, mostly for a handful of items. The most fine-grained test so far used a perceptual task: @imhoff2023 [Study 2] showed participants dot patterns of about 500 dots next to standards labelled with their exact number of dots, which differed from the target by up to 400 dots in 20-dot steps. Estimates were drawn towards these symbolic anchors, but the pull levelled off once the anchor differed from the target by more than about 300 dots.

The two recent meta-analyses reach different conclusions. Using the Open Anchoring Quest (OpAQ) data, @roseler2022meta found that Hedges' *g* increased with the relative distance between anchor and true value and concluded against the prediction that extreme anchors produce smaller effects. @schley2026 coded extremity as a binary flag, mainly for anchors that the original authors described as extreme or implausible, and found no difference in effect size. @barrera2024 modelled the anchored crowd mean as a weighted average of anchor and crowd mean, with a weight that decays exponentially with the distance between anchor and truth, and found that this weight fell with distance across 30 percentage questions.

These results are hard to compare because they measure anchor influence in different units. A standardised mean difference between high- and low-anchor conditions rises with the distance between the anchors even if every anchor pulls estimates by the same proportion of its distance. A finding that *g* grows with anchor distance is therefore compatible with constant, rising and falling proportional influence. The theories speak to the proportional pull: how much of the distance between belief and anchor is carried into the estimate. @jacowitz1995 captured this with the anchoring index, the difference between median estimates under high and low anchors divided by the difference between the anchors, and @roseler2022meta called for such a unitless measure "to formalize the relationship between anchor distance and adjustment strength" [@roseler2022meta, p. 34].

## Process models and their predictions

We consider five process models. Each maps an anchor and a belief onto an estimate, and each implies a shape for the relation between anchor extremity and proportional pull ([@fig-models]). The models are specific formal implementations, all defined on the log scale of the estimated quantity; a test of one of them is a test of that implementation, not of every version of the theory that inspired it.

In *anchor-and-adjust with a fixed number of adjustments* (M1), people start at the anchor and adjust towards their belief in a limited number of stochastic steps. This is not a theory anyone has defended in its own right; it is the mechanistic core of the resource-rational account with the number of adjustments held constant, as in Lieder et al.'s fit to Jacowitz and Kahneman's data (29 adjustments), and it shows what adjustment alone implies. @lieder2018a formalised adjustment as a Metropolis-Hastings chain that starts at the anchor and moves towards the belief distribution. When the anchor is far away, each step covers a bounded distance, so a fixed number of steps leaves a larger share of the distance uncorrected, and the proportional pull rises with extremity. Lieder et al. approximated the chain's convergence as geometric, which implies a constant proportional pull (their Eq. 4); that approximation holds for anchors near the belief, and our simulations use the chain itself.

In *resource-rational anchor-and-adjust* (M1R), the number of adjustments is chosen to minimise expected error plus a time cost per adjustment [@lieder2018a, Eq. 2]. Anchors inside the plausible range are barely adjusted, because adjusting from them buys little accuracy, while far anchors justify many adjustments. The resulting pull can fall with extremity, but its shape depends on the time cost and on how uncertain people are.

In *constant-weight integration* (M2), the estimate is a weighted average of anchor and belief with a fixed weight. This is the simplest version of the anchor integration model [@turner2016], and in log units it implies a constant proportional pull. It is the null model for shape. A constant weight on the raw scale would instead imply a declining log-scale elasticity for anchors below the belief and a rising one above it; we examine this variant in an exploratory analysis.

In *adjustment to the plausible boundary* (M3), people accept anchors that lie inside the range of values they find plausible and adjust from implausible anchors only until they reach the edge of that range [@mussweiler2001; @epley2006]. @epley2006 proposed this stopping rule for self-generated anchors; M3 applies it to provided anchors. Beyond the boundary the estimate stops moving, so the proportional pull falls towards zero.

In *plausibility-discounted integration* (M4), the anchor's weight declines as the anchor becomes implausible. This formalises the proposal that extreme anchors lose influence because they are implausible [@wegener2001], and it resembles the anchor integration model, in which an anchor's influence depends on how consistent it is with prior beliefs [@turner2016]. Selective-accessibility accounts, in which anchoring arises from anchor-consistent knowledge activated during the comparison [@strack1997; @mussweiler1999], have been read as predicting smaller effects for implausible anchors [@roseler2022meta]. The pull falls, and far enough out, a more extreme anchor moves the estimate back towards the belief.

The models also include a no-anchoring baseline (M0). Lieder et al. derived that bias grows linearly with anchor distance when the number of adjustments is fixed, showed how the optimal number of adjustments depends on distance, and fitted a five-level anchoring demonstration in which bias rose linearly with the anchor, but did not examine whether proportional influence changes for implausibly extreme anchors. @turner2016 built an inverted U between anchor extremity and the size of the shift in estimates into their model "for simplicity" and tested it with one anchor per item.

## The present study

We tested these predictions on OpAQ, an openly licensed collection of trial-level anchoring data [@roseler2022opaq]. Because anchor values in most studies were chosen by the original authors together with the items, a comparison across items confounds extremity with item properties. Our primary test is therefore within items: in studies that presented many different anchors for the same question, we asked how the proportional pull changes as the anchor moves away from the true value. Compared with the dot-estimation evidence of @imhoff2023, these studies use general-knowledge magnitudes and anchors that lie up to several orders of magnitude from the true value. A comparison of the anchoring index across two-anchor studies is a secondary test. We simulated every model on the exact OpAQ designs to derive numeric predictions and passed the simulated data through the same estimators as the observed data. We preregistered the predictions, decision rules and analyses before reading any estimate.

Estimates entered the analysis if the anchor was explicitly random, fixed, or relevant to the target (self-generated and incidental anchors were excluded); the response scale was open; the quantity was a positive ratio-scale magnitude (e.g., a length, price, population or count, but not a date, temperature, percentage or preference); and anchor and true value were positive. ## Measures

For every estimate we computed *y* = ln(estimate / true value) and *x* = ln(anchor / true value). Working on the log scale treats a doubling of a height and a doubling of a population alike and matches the roughly log-normal spread of numeric estimates. The log elasticity, the change in *y* per unit change in *x*, is a unitless proportional pull: an elasticity of .5 means that doubling the anchor multiplies the estimate by about 1.41.

In the within-item set we modelled *y* = *a*~cell~ + *b*·*x* + *g*·*x*|*x*|. Here *b* is the fitted local elasticity at the true value (for an average cell), and the curvature *g* describes how the local elasticity, *b* + 2*g*|*x*|, changes as the anchor moves away from the true value in either direction. The local elasticity is the proportional change in the estimate per proportional change in the anchor at a given anchor value; it is not the share of the whole distance between belief and anchor that ends up in the estimate. We also report the relative curvature ρ = *g*/*b*, which does not depend on the overall strength of anchoring. In the across-cell set we computed each cell's log anchoring index, the difference between the median *y* under the high and the low anchor divided by the log ratio of the anchors, and each cell's extremity, the mean absolute log distance of its two anchors from the true value. The standard error of a median was approximated as 1.2533 × MAD / √*n*, where MAD is the median absolute deviation scaled by 1.4826 to estimate the standard deviation (the R default), and the standard error of the index as the square root of the summed squared standard errors of the two medians, divided by the log ratio of the anchors. No participant answered under both anchors of the same cell, so the two medians are independent.

## Model predictions

The five process models and the no-anchoring baseline were implemented on the log scale ([@fig-models]; specification in `R/models.R`). Every participant-item combination had a belief centre drawn around the true value, with item-level bias and between-person spread. Responses included response noise and a 2% share of gross errors. Model parameters are expressed in units of the item's belief uncertainty σ, which was drawn from 0.3 to 1.2 log units per item.

To fix the models' parameters without using OpAQ outcomes, we calibrated each model to the anchoring index that @jacowitz1995 reported for anchors at the 15th and 85th percentiles of unanchored estimates (about .49), accepting parameter values that produced an index between .30 and .60. The preregistered calibration computed this index on the log scale; a raw-scale recalibration is reported as a sensitivity analysis. The number of accepted grid points per model was `r paste(sprintf("%s: %d", acc$model, acc$N), collapse = "; ")`. We then simulated each model on the exact OpAQ designs (the same anchors, true values, participants and cell sizes; `r n_rep[model == "M0"]$N` replicates for M0 and `r n_rep[model == "M1"]$N` for each other model), drawing parameters uniformly from the accepted grid points, and passed each simulated dataset through the estimators used for the observed data. [@tbl-predictions] lists the resulting predictions.

M1R's curvature depends on its parameters, with a predictive interval spanning zero. The across-cell slope follows the same pattern.

## Analysis plan

**H1 (primary).** In the within-item set we fitted a linear mixed model with fixed effects for *x* and *x*|*x*|, uncorrelated random intercepts, slopes and curvatures by cell, and random intercepts by participant, using lme4 and lmerTest [@bates2015; @kuznetsova2017] in R [@rcore2026]. Confidence intervals for *b* and *g* used Satterthwaite degrees of freedom; the interval for ρ used a delta-method standard error. Estimates were removed as gross errors when their log distance from the true value exceeded both ln(1000) and the cell's largest anchor distance plus ln(10), a rule that never removes a response equal to an anchor. H1a and H1b applied the same model to the random-anchor and fixed-anchor strata.

**Decision rules.** The shape test was interpreted only if the confidence interval for *b* lay above zero (gate G1). We then classified the curvature, in this order, as *flat* if the confidence interval for ρ lay within the equivalence bounds ±0.05, as *rising* if the interval for *g* lay above zero, as *falling* if it lay below zero, and otherwise as inconclusive. Using a 95% interval for this check amounts to an equivalence test at α = .025 [@lakens2017]; the bounds sit just below the smallest relative curvature in the 95% predictive interval of M1, M3 and M4 and far outside that of M2. Applied to the simulated replicates, this rule labelled data generated by M1 as rising in more than 99% of replicates, data from M3 and M4 as falling in more than 99%, data from M2 as flat in more than 99%, and data from M0 as failing the gate in all replicates. These operating characteristics are approximations: they use normal critical values, always the full random-effects structure, and a simplified version of gate G2.

**H2 (secondary).** We regressed the cell-level log anchoring index on extremity in a multilevel meta-regression with random intercepts for studies and cells within studies [@viechtbauer2010], using standard errors derived from the median absolute deviation (MAD) of each condition. Gate G2 required the mean index to exceed zero; the slope *d* was classified with the same ordered rule and equivalence bounds of ±0.03.

**H3 (model adequacy).** A model was contradicted when the observed curvature (*g* or ρ) or the across-cell slope *d* fell outside its 95% predictive interval; M0 was also contradicted if gate G1 passed. The observed level of anchoring (*b* and the mean index) was compared with each model's interval but did not decide survival, because levels inherit the calibration to Jacowitz and Kahneman's design.

**Robustness.** We preregistered seven robustness analyses: median regression without the gross-error rule, with a participant-cluster bootstrap [@koenker1978; @quantreg]; separate slopes for near (|*x*| ≤ 1) and far anchors; H1 without @bahnik2021; H2 with the raw-scale anchoring index; H2 with design covariates; H2 without one study whose item coding may contain errors; and two alternative extremity measures.

## Deviations from the preregistration

We made four changes after the confirmatory analysis had been run. First, a code review found that the observed mean anchoring index in the H3 level check was computed with a different estimator from the simulated one; we replaced it with the same inverse-variance weighted mean. This affects only level criteria, which do not decide model survival. Second, the preregistration described one M1R parameter incorrectly; the code, and therefore the predictions, were correct. Third, we made code changes that altered no reported number, and we disclose two numerical safeguards that were in the preregistered code but not in its text (a floor for the MAD and the exclusion of cells with zero standard error in one robustness analysis); neither affected the analysed data. Fourth, we clarified that the relative-curvature interval uses a normal critical value. One cell (Shanks et al., 2020, Study 3, the population of Chicago) was excluded in full: its participants answered in millions, while its anchors and true value were raw counts, so all of its responses exceeded the preregistered gross-error limit. All analyses labelled exploratory or sensitivity were added after the preregistration.

(A simple inverse-variance weighted mean, which gives most weight to a few very precise cells, is `r f3(w_ai)`; we use it only to compare with the simulations, which computed the same quantity.) The slope of the index on extremity was *d* = `r f3(h2$slope)`, `r ci(h2$slope_lo, h2$slope_hi)`. This interval includes zero but is not narrow enough to establish equivalence within ±0.03, so the result is inconclusive under the preregistered rule. Because the standard error of a cell's index is inversely proportional to the log distance between its anchors, cells with widely spaced anchors, which also tend to be the more extreme cells, receive more weight ([@fig-across], panel A). The point estimate is positive, the opposite sign to the within-item curvature.
218
