221	#| fig-cap: "Across-cell relation between anchor extremity and anchor influence. (A) Log anchoring index per cell with the preregistered meta-regression line and 95% confidence band. (B) Hedges' *g* per cell (exploratory). Point area is proportional to 1/SE of each cell's estimate. The standardised effect rises with extremity, while the proportional index does not change detectably. Figure produced with R code written by an AI system (see Method)."
222	knitr::include_graphics(here("manuscript", "figures", "fig3_across_cells.png"))
223	```
224	
225	## Model adequacy (H3)
226	
227	[@tbl-h3] compares the observed statistics with each model's predictive interval. M1 predicts positive curvature and is contradicted by the negative observed curvature. M2 predicts no curvature and is contradicted as well. M3 and M4 predict negative curvature and contain the observed *g* in their intervals, but they predict stronger relative curvature than observed (their intervals for ρ lie below `r f2(max(pi_("M3", "rho_hi"), pi_("M4", "rho_hi")))`) and a clearly negative across-cell slope, which the data do not show. The preregistered survival rule retains a model if the observed across-cell slope falls inside its interval and at least one of the two curvature statistics (*g* or ρ) does; ρ was included so that a model whose overall anchoring strength was mis-calibrated could still pass on shape. Under this rule, only M1R survived. This does not mean that M1R predicted the data well: the observed *g* lay outside its interval, and M1R passed only because its interval for ρ was very wide (`r ci(pi_("M1R", "rho_lo"), pi_("M1R", "rho_hi"), 2)`), mainly because some of its parameter settings produce almost no anchoring. On the within-item curvature alone, M3 and M4 were the models whose intervals contained the observed value. In a post-hoc joint check, `r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * rj[model == "M3"]$share_b_and_g_inside)` of M3's and `r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * rj[model == "M4"]$share_b_and_g_inside)` of M4's replicates produced both *b* and *g* inside the observed confidence intervals, compared with none for M1, M1R and M2; M1R is therefore best described as not supported by the within-item data. The across-cell slope compares items whose anchors were chosen by researchers, so a model's failure to predict it is weaker evidence against that model than a failure to predict the within-item curvature.
228	
229	```{r tbl-h3}
230	#| tbl-cap: "Observed statistics compared with each model's 95% predictive interval. Each cell shows whether the observed value lies inside (in) or outside (out) the model's interval, followed by the interval. Under the preregistered rule a model is retained if d and at least one of g and ρ lie inside its intervals. M3 and M4 contained the observed g and were rejected only because of the across-cell slope d; M1R was retained although the observed g lay outside its interval, because its interval for ρ was very wide."
231	obs <- c(g = P$g, rho = P$rho, d = h2$slope, b = P$b, ai = w_ai)
232	t3 <- merge(pint, h3, by = "model")
233	t3 <- t3[, .(Model = model,
234	             `Curvature g` = sprintf("%s %s", ifelse(g_inside, "in", "out"), ci(g_lo, g_hi)),
235	             `Relative curvature ρ` = ifelse(model == "M0", "—", sprintf("%s %s", ifelse(rho_inside, "in", "out"), ci(rho_lo, rho_hi, 2))),
236	             `Across-cell slope d` = sprintf("%s %s", ifelse(slope_inside, "in", "out"), ci(slope_lo, slope_hi)),
237	             Retained = ifelse(survives_shape, "yes", "no"))]
238	t3[, Model := c(M0 = "M0 No anchoring", M1 = "M1 Anchor-and-adjust, fixed", M1R = "M1R Anchor-and-adjust, resource-rational",
239	                M2 = "M2 Constant weight", M3 = "M3 Plausible boundary", M4 = "M4 Plausibility discount")[Model]]
240	knitr::kable(t3)
241	```
242	
243	Observed values were *g* = `r f3(obs["g"])`, ρ = `r f2(obs["rho"])` and *d* = `r f3(obs["d"])`. For the level criteria, the observed elasticity at the true value (*b* = `r f3(obs["b"])`) lay inside the intervals of `r paste(h3[b_inside == TRUE]$model, collapse = ", ")`, and both *b* and the weighted mean log anchoring index (`r f3(obs["ai"])`) lay inside the intervals of `r paste(h3[survives_level == TRUE]$model, collapse = " and ")` only.
244	
245	## Robustness
246	
247	The within-item result held in the preregistered robustness analyses that retained the random-anchor data. Median regression without the gross-error rule gave *g* = `r f3(r_("R1_median_regression_g"))`, `r ci(r_("R1_median_regression_g", "lo"), r_("R1_median_regression_g", "hi"))`. Replacing the curvature term by separate slopes for near and far anchors showed that the slope for anchors more than one log unit from the true value differed from the slope near the true value by `r f2(r_("R2_far_minus_near_slope"))`, `r ci(r_("R2_far_minus_near_slope", "lo"), r_("R2_far_minus_near_slope", "hi"), 2)`; the slope was `r f2(rc_("R1b_near_slope"))`, `r ci(rc_("R1b_near_slope", "lo"), rc_("R1b_near_slope", "hi"), 2)`, near the true value and `r f2(rc_("R1b_far_slope"))`, `r ci(rc_("R1b_far_slope", "lo"), rc_("R1b_far_slope", "hi"), 2)`, further away, so far anchors still pulled estimates, but less (both reported post hoc). Without @bahnik2021 the estimate was similar but very imprecise, *g* = `r f3(r_("R3_without_bahnik_g"))`, `r ci(r_("R3_without_bahnik_g", "lo"), r_("R3_without_bahnik_g", "hi"), 2)`.
248	
249	The across-cell slope stayed positive and imprecise in most checks: with design covariates, *d* = `r f3(r_("R5_covariates_slope"))`, `r ci(r_("R5_covariates_slope", "lo"), r_("R5_covariates_slope", "hi"))`; with the largest anchor distance as the extremity measure, `r f3(r_("R7_max_distance_slope"))`, `r ci(r_("R7_max_distance_slope", "lo"), r_("R7_max_distance_slope", "hi"))`; with the log ratio of the anchors, `r f3(r_("R7_log_spread_slope"))`, `r ci(r_("R7_log_spread_slope", "lo"), r_("R7_log_spread_slope", "hi"))`. Without Weber et al. (2021), a study from the OpAQ team whose item coding may be affected by item mix-ups that an unpublished 2026 corrigendum reported for a related publication, the slope was `r f3(r_("R6_without_weber_slope"))`, `r ci(r_("R6_without_weber_slope", "lo"), r_("R6_without_weber_slope", "hi"))`, the only check in which the interval excluded zero. The raw-scale anchoring index, which the preregistration designated as descriptive because a constant log-scale weight does not imply a constant raw-scale index, gave `r f3(r_("R4_raw_index_slope"))`, `r ci(r_("R4_raw_index_slope", "lo"), r_("R4_raw_index_slope", "hi"))`.
250	
251	## Exploratory analyses
252	
253	The following analyses were not preregistered.
254	
255	*Both sides of the true value.* The curvature was negative both for anchors below the true value, *g* = `r f3(x_("E1_xx_neg"))`, `r ci(x_("E1_xx_neg", "lo"), x_("E1_xx_neg", "hi"))`, and for anchors above it, *g* = `r f3(x_("E1_xx_pos"))`, `r ci(x_("E1_xx_pos", "lo"), x_("E1_xx_pos", "hi"))`.
256	
257	*Item by item.* In each of the `r e2[!is.na(diff), .N]` cells with at least 20 estimates both within and beyond one log unit of the true value (the 13 cells of @bahnik2021, the Cologne cathedral item and one of the two items of @yoon2021), the slope for far anchors was lower than the slope for near anchors (median difference `r f2(median(e2$diff, na.rm = TRUE))`). The other Yoon et al. item had too few near anchors for this analysis; the positive curvature reported below for the two Yoon et al. items together comes from a different specification (a quadratic fit to both items together, including the item not in this comparison).
258	
259	*Standardised effect sizes.* Across cells, Hedges' *g* rose with extremity by `r f2(x_("E3_hedges_g_slope"))` per log unit, `r ci(x_("E3_hedges_g_slope", "lo"), x_("E3_hedges_g_slope", "hi"), 2)` ([@fig-across], panel B), in line with @roseler2022meta. The same cells therefore show a rising standardised effect and no detectable change in proportional pull.
260	
261	*Extremity relative to response spread.* The across-cell extremity measure ignores how uncertain people are about each quantity. When we divided extremity by the spread of log estimates within each anchor condition (a measure that is itself affected by anchoring), the slope turned negative, *d* = `r f3(x_("E4_slope_on_scaled_extremity"))`, `r ci(x_("E4_slope_on_scaled_extremity", "lo"), x_("E4_slope_on_scaled_extremity", "hi"))`. When we instead entered extremity and spread as separate predictors, the extremity slope was `r f3(x_("E4_slope_adjusting_spread"))`, `r ci(x_("E4_slope_adjusting_spread", "lo"), x_("E4_slope_adjusting_spread", "hi"))`. The two specifications disagree, and a ratio predictor can produce spurious associations when its denominator is related to the outcome's precision, so this analysis does not settle whether the across-cell pattern reflects how anchors were placed relative to people's uncertainty.
262	
263	*Relaxed calibration.* To check whether the model failures stem from the calibration to Jacowitz and Kahneman's index, we drew 300 parameter sets per model from wide ranges without calibration and simulated each on the OpAQ designs. None of these draws reproduced the observed *b*, *g*, *d* and mean index jointly (all four inside their observed 95% confidence intervals); with 300 draws per model, this shows that such parameter settings are rare, not that none exist. Within-item *b* and *g* together were reproduced by `r e5[model == "M4"]$within_b_and_g` of 300 M4 draws, `r e5[model == "M1R"]$within_b_and_g` M1R draws and `r e5[model == "M3"]$within_b_and_g` M3 draws, and by no M1 or M2 draw; the across-cell *d* and mean index together were reproduced by `r e5[model == "M2"]$across_d_and_ai` M2 draws, `r e5[model == "M1"]$across_d_and_ai` M1 draws and `r e5[model == "M1R"]$across_d_and_ai` M1R draws, and by no M3 or M4 draw.
264	
265	*Constant weight on the raw scale.* M2 assumes a constant weight on the log scale. We also simulated a constant weight on the raw scale (the estimate is a weighted average of anchor and belief in raw units; weights drawn from .30 to .60; 300 replicates). Passed through the H1 estimator, this model predicted a negative pooled curvature, *g* = `r f3(e6_("g"))`, `r ci(e6_("g", "lo"), e6_("g", "hi"))`, an interval that contains the observed value, because on the log scale raw averaging flattens the response to anchors below the belief. It predicted opposite curvatures on the two sides of the true value, however: negative below (`r f3(e6_("g_below"))`, `r ci(e6_("g_below", "lo"), e6_("g_below", "hi"))`) and positive above (`r f3(e6_("g_above"))`, `r ci(e6_("g_above", "lo"), e6_("g_above", "hi"))`). The observed curvature above the true value was negative (`r f3(x_("E1_xx_pos"))`), which contradicts raw-scale constant weighting. The preregistered pooled test alone would not have ruled out this model.
266	
267	*Study-specific estimates.* The curvature was negative in @bahnik2021, *g* = `r f3(rc_("R1c_g_Bahník, 2021a"))`, `r ci(rc_("R1c_g_Bahník, 2021a", "lo"), rc_("R1c_g_Bahník, 2021a", "hi"))`, and in the Cologne cathedral item of @imhoff2023, `r f3(rc_("R1c_g_Imhoff & Barker, 2022, Study 2"))`, `r ci(rc_("R1c_g_Imhoff & Barker, 2022, Study 2", "lo"), rc_("R1c_g_Imhoff & Barker, 2022, Study 2", "hi"))`; it was imprecise in Frech et al. (2021), `r f3(rc_("R1c_g_Frech et al., 2021"))`, `r ci(rc_("R1c_g_Frech et al., 2021", "lo"), rc_("R1c_g_Frech et al., 2021", "hi"), 2)`, and positive in the two items of @yoon2021, whose anchors were participants' own height or age, `r f3(rc_("R1c_g_Yoon et al., 2021, Form C"))`, `r ci(rc_("R1c_g_Yoon et al., 2021, Form C", "lo"), rc_("R1c_g_Yoon et al., 2021, Form C", "hi"))`. @imhoff2023 reported a linear relation between anchor and estimate for the Cologne cathedral item on the raw scale; a linear raw-scale relation also produces a declining log-scale elasticity for anchors below the belief, so this item alone does not discriminate between log-scale plausibility models and raw-scale averaging.
268	
269	## Sensitivity analyses
270	
271	These analyses were added after a code review and were not preregistered.
272	
273	*Calibration scale.* The preregistered calibration compared the models' log-scale anchoring index with Jacowitz and Kahneman's value of about .49, which they computed on the raw scale. Recalibrating every model to a raw-scale index accepted largely the same parameter values (`r paste(sprintf("%s: %d of %d", s1acc$model, s1acc$both, s1acc$log_scale), collapse = "; ")` of the originally accepted grid points were also accepted), and new predictions from the recalibrated models led to the same conclusion: only M1R survived the shape criteria.
274	
275	*Dependence on single studies (H1).* Leaving out any one of the three smaller studies left the curvature negative with confidence intervals excluding zero (*g* from `r f3(min(s_("S2_without_Frech et al., 2021"), s_("S2_without_Yoon et al., 2021, Form C"), s_("S2_without_Imhoff & Barker, 2022, Study 2")))` to `r f3(max(s_("S2_without_Frech et al., 2021"), s_("S2_without_Yoon et al., 2021, Form C"), s_("S2_without_Imhoff & Barker, 2022, Study 2")))`). Adding study-level random effects gave *g* = `r f3(s_("S2_study_random_effect"))`, `r ci(s_("S2_study_random_effect", "lo"), s_("S2_study_random_effect", "hi"))`. The single fixed-anchor item with 20 anchor levels [the supplementary task of @imhoff2023, Study 2] showed a negative curvature on its own, *g* = `r f3(s_("S2_imhoff_barker_only"))`, `r ci(s_("S2_imhoff_barker_only", "lo"), s_("S2_imhoff_barker_only", "hi"))`.
276	
277	*Influence and clustering (H2).* The across-cell slope was not robust. With study-clustered robust standard errors, *d* = `r f3(s_("S3_cluster_robust_slope"))`, `r ci(s_("S3_cluster_robust_slope", "lo"), s_("S3_cluster_robust_slope", "hi"))`. The ten most precise cells carried `r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * s_("S3_top10_weight_share"))` of the inverse-variance weight; without them, *d* = `r f3(s_("S3_without_top10_weight_cells"))`, `r ci(s_("S3_without_top10_weight_cells", "lo"), s_("S3_without_top10_weight_cells", "hi"))`. Leaving out one study at a time gave slopes between `r f3(s_("S3_loo_slope_range", "lo"))` and `r f3(s_("S3_loo_slope_range", "hi"))`. Resampling participants within studies gave a median slope of `r f3(rc_("R1d_h2_slope_participant_bootstrap"))` (this interval, `r ci(rc_("R1d_h2_slope_participant_bootstrap", "lo"), rc_("R1d_h2_slope_participant_bootstrap", "hi"))`, reflects participant sampling only, not variation between items), and converting the Chicago responses from millions and retaining that cell gave *d* = `r f3(rc_("R1e_h2_slope_chicago_converted"))`, `r ci(rc_("R1e_h2_slope_chicago_converted", "lo"), rc_("R1e_h2_slope_chicago_converted", "hi"))`.
278	
279	# Discussion
280	
281	Within items, estimates responded less to changes in the anchor as the anchor moved away from the true value. Near the truth, the local elasticity was `r f2(P$b)`; for anchors a factor of 2.7 from the truth it was `r f2(loc_el(1))`, and for anchors a factor of 7.4 away, `r f2(loc_el(2))`. The decline appeared on both sides of the true value, in every item with enough near and far anchors, and in the one fixed-anchor item with many anchor levels. Across two-anchor studies, where authors chose one anchor pair per item, the anchoring index showed no detectable decline, and its point estimate leaned the other way.
282	
283	## What the within-item result rules out
284	
285	The negative curvature contradicts two simple implementations. Anchor-and-adjust with a fixed number of steps predicts that far anchors keep more of their distance, because a bounded number of bounded steps cannot correct a large gap; the data show the reverse. Constant-weight integration on the log scale predicts no change in proportional pull; it too is contradicted. Constant weighting on the raw scale predicts the observed pooled curvature, but also a rising elasticity above the true value, which the exploratory side-specific estimates contradict. The implementations that predict a decline on both sides share one feature: the anchor's influence is limited by how plausible it is. The within-item shape is consistent with this feature, but the calibrated versions of these models did not reproduce the data quantitatively, so plausibility-limited influence is one possible account rather than an established mechanism. This holds for adjustment that stops at the edge of the plausible range [@mussweiler2001; @epley2006] and for integration that discounts implausible anchors [@wegener2001; @turner2016]. The resource-rational variant can also produce a decline, but its calibrated versions did not reproduce the observed combination of elasticity and curvature. The result fits earlier experiments with few anchor levels in which implausible anchors had proportionally smaller effects [@chapman1994; @mussweiler2001; @wegener2001], the distance-decaying anchoring weight of @barrera2024, and the levelling-off of assimilation to symbolic anchors in dot estimation [@imhoff2023]. It extends these findings to general-knowledge magnitudes, to anchors far outside the plausible range, and to a proportional outcome. In a dot-estimation task with anchors 35% or 70% away from the true value, the more distant anchors produced larger estimation errors [@mayer2024]; a larger absolute effect is compatible with a declining proportional pull, so the two findings do not conflict.
286	
287	Relative to the overall strength of anchoring, the decline was smaller than the calibrated versions of M3 and M4 predicted: their intervals for ρ lay below the observed value, and far anchors still had a positive slope. Far anchors thus pulled estimates more than a hard plausibility boundary or a steep plausibility discount allows, at least within the calibrated parameter ranges. A mixture in which the weight of an anchor falls gradually but does not vanish could describe this. The data do not identify such a model, and we did not test one.
288	
289	## The across-cell pattern
290	
291	The across-cell analysis did not reproduce the within-item decline, and no model with a single parameter set reproduced both patterns. Two explanations are plausible, and our data cannot fully separate them. First, extremity measured against the true value is not extremity measured against people's uncertainty. Researchers may place anchors further from the truth for quantities that people know poorly. An anchor ten times the true population of a city may be less implausible than an anchor twice the height of a familiar building. When we scaled extremity by the spread of estimates, the across-cell slope turned negative, as the within-item analysis and the plausibility accounts predict, but entering spread as a separate predictor left the extremity slope positive and imprecise. Because the spread is itself affected by anchoring, neither analysis resolves the question. Second, the two sets differ in anchor type: the within-item set is mostly random anchors, and the across-cell set only fixed or relevant anchors. The models make the same shape predictions for both, but it is possible that informative anchors lose less pull with extremity than anchors people know to be random. The fixed-anchor stratum of the within-item set pointed in the same direction as the random-anchor stratum but was too small for the preregistered test, and only one fixed-anchor item had enough anchor levels to show the decline on its own.
292	
293	The divergence also bears on how moderator analyses of anchoring should be read. In the same cells, the standardised effect rose with extremity while the proportional index did not change detectably. Meta-analytic findings that larger anchor distances produce larger standardised effects [@roseler2022meta] therefore say little about whether extreme anchors are more influential per unit of distance. Tests of anchoring theories need a proportional outcome and variation in extremity that the researcher controls.
294	
295	## Limitations
296	
297	The primary evidence rests largely on one study. Thirteen of the 20 within-item cells, and `r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * wct[study == "Bahník, 2021a", sum(estimates)] / P$n_rows)` of the within-item estimates, come from @bahnik2021, in which participants compared 13 random anchors with 13 different lengths and heights. Without this study the within-item curvature had the same sign but a confidence interval too wide to be informative. The random anchors also differ from the fixed anchors that dominate applied settings. The preregistered test of the fixed-anchor stratum was not informative; in an exploratory analysis, the one fixed-anchor item with 20 anchor levels showed the same decline, but it is a single item. A direct test of the extremity function for informative anchors needs experiments that present many anchor levels for many items.
298	
299	Second, extremity was measured relative to the true value, not relative to each participant's belief. Where people systematically over- or underestimate a quantity, the anchor's distance from their belief differs from its distance from the truth. The simulations included item-level bias to account for this, and the curvature was negative on both sides of the true value. However, a study that elicits unanchored estimates or plausible ranges from the same participants would give a cleaner measure.
300	
301	Third, the models were specified on the log scale and calibrated to a single external benchmark. The shape predictions of M1, M2, M3 and M4 follow from their structure and held across all calibrated parameter values, but the level predictions depend on the calibration, and the resource-rational model's predictions depend strongly on its time cost and on how uncertain people are. That this model survived our tests reflects the width of its predictions more than a close fit. Formal tests of resource-rational anchoring need independent measures of the time cost and of people's uncertainty.
302	
303	Fourth, OpAQ harmonises data from many studies, and its codes do not always match the original designs: the two items of @yoon2021 used participants' own height or age as anchors, and the anchors of the Cologne cathedral item were described by its authors as random. Harmonisation can also introduce errors. We found one item whose responses were recorded in different units from its anchors and true value, and an unpublished 2026 corrigendum, posted on the OpAQ project page for a related publication by the same group, suggests that the item coding of another study (Weber et al., 2021) may contain errors. Our rules removed the first; excluding the second made the across-cell slope positive and significant. We used only positive ratio-scale quantities with open response scales, so the results do not speak to dates, percentages, bounded scales or preferences.
304	
305	## Conclusion
306	
307	Within the same questions, estimates responded less to changes in the anchor when the anchor was far from the true value than when it was close to it. The evidence comes mostly from random anchors for lengths and heights in one study, with the same pattern in the one fixed-anchor item that had many anchor levels. It contradicts anchor-and-adjust with a fixed number of steps and constant-weight integration, and is consistent with accounts in which an anchor's influence is limited by its plausibility. No calibrated model, however, explained the combined results: the plausibility models predicted a steeper within-item decline and a falling across-cell trend. Across studies with researcher-chosen anchors, the pattern was not visible. Whether deliberately chosen, informative anchors, such as opening offers in negotiations, also show diminishing returns to extremity cannot be answered with these data. The extremity function should be estimated within items, with proportional measures and with anchors of the kind used in practice.
308

The across-cell analysis included `r h2$n_cells` cells and `r nf(h2$n_rows)` estimates; `r nf(excl[set == "across"]$invalid_estimate)` estimates were missing or non-positive and `r nf(excl[set == "across"]$gross_error)` were removed as gross errors, `r nf(870)` of them from the cell with the unit mismatch.

## Within items, the proportional pull falls with extremity (H1)

Anchoring was clearly present in the within-item set: the local elasticity at the true value was *b* = `r f3(P$b)`, 95% CI `r ci(P$b_lo, P$b_hi)`, so doubling the anchor raised estimates by about `r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * (2^P$b - 1))` near the true value. The curvature was negative, *g* = `r f3(P$g)`, `r ci(P$g_lo, P$g_hi)`, *t*(`r f2(P$g_df, 1)`) = `r f2(P$g / ((P$g_hi - P$g_lo) / (2 * qt(.975, P$g_df))))`, *p* `r if (P$g_p < .001) "< .001" else paste("=", sprintf("%.3f", P$g_p))`, with a relative curvature of ρ = `r f2(P$rho)`, `r ci(P$rho_lo, P$rho_hi, 2)`. By the preregistered rule, the elasticity *falls* with extremity. The fitted local elasticity *b* + 2*g*|*x*| was `r f2(loc_el(1))` for anchors one log unit (a factor of 2.7) from the true value and `r f2(loc_el(2))` for anchors two log units (a factor of 7.4) away, about half its value at the true value. For a quantity whose true value is 100, the fitted curve (ignoring item-specific terms) implies that doubling the anchor from 50 to 100 raises the median estimate by `r dbl(50)`, doubling it from 200 to 400 by `r dbl(200)`, and doubling it from 500 to 1,000 by `r dbl(500)`. Because the curvature term is quadratic, the fitted local elasticity would turn negative beyond |*x*| = `r f2(P$b / (2 * abs(P$g)))` (a factor of `r sprintf("%.0f", exp(P$b / (2 * abs(P$g))))`), where few anchors lie; this turning point is a property of the functional form, and the piecewise analysis below, which has no turning point, shows the same flattening. [@fig-within] shows the binned observed estimates and the fitted curves for each cell.

In the random-anchor stratum the result was the same: *b* = `r f3(R$b)`, `r ci(R$b_lo, R$b_hi)`, and *g* = `r f3(R$g)`, `r ci(R$g_lo, R$g_hi)`, again classified as falling. In this stratum the full model did not converge, and the preregistered fallback removed the between-cell variance of the curvature. The curvature is then estimated as common to all cells, which inflates its degrees of freedom (`r nf(round(R$g_df))`) and makes its interval narrower than one that allowed the curvature to vary between items. In the fixed-anchor stratum the point estimates were similar (*b* = `r f3(FX$b)`, *g* = `r f3(FX$g)`, `r ci(FX$g_lo, FX$g_hi)`), but with only five cells the confidence interval for *b* spanned `r ci(FX$b_lo, FX$b_hi, 2)`, so the gate failed and the shape was not testable there under the preregistered rules.

## Across cells, the anchoring index shows no clear trend (H2)

## Model adequacy (H3)

[@tbl-h3] compares the observed statistics with each model's predictive interval. M1 predicts positive curvature and is contradicted by the negative observed curvature. M2 predicts no curvature and is contradicted as well. M3 and M4 predict negative curvature and contain the observed *g* in their intervals, but they predict stronger relative curvature than observed (their intervals for ρ lie below `r f2(max(pi_("M3", "rho_hi"), pi_("M4", "rho_hi")))`) and a clearly negative across-cell slope, which the data do not show. The preregistered survival rule retains a model if the observed across-cell slope falls inside its interval and at least one of the two curvature statistics (*g* or ρ) does; ρ was included so that a model whose overall anchoring strength was mis-calibrated could still pass on shape. Under this rule, only M1R survived. This does not mean that M1R predicted the data well: the observed *g* lay outside its interval, and M1R passed only because its interval for ρ was very wide (`r ci(pi_("M1R", "rho_lo"), pi_("M1R", "rho_hi"), 2)`), mainly because some of its parameter settings produce almost no anchoring. On the within-item curvature alone, M3 and M4 were the models whose intervals contained the observed value. In a post-hoc joint check, `r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * rj[model == "M3"]$share_b_and_g_inside)` of M3's and `r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * rj[model == "M4"]$share_b_and_g_inside)` of M4's replicates produced both *b* and *g* inside the observed confidence intervals, compared with none for M1, M1R and M2; M1R is therefore best described as not supported by the within-item data. The across-cell slope compares items whose anchors were chosen by researchers, so a model's failure to predict it is weaker evidence against that model than a failure to predict the within-item curvature.

## Exploratory analyses

The following analyses were not preregistered.

*Both sides of the true value.* The curvature was negative both for anchors below the true value, *g* = `r f3(x_("E1_xx_neg"))`, `r ci(x_("E1_xx_neg", "lo"), x_("E1_xx_neg", "hi"))`, and for anchors above it, *g* = `r f3(x_("E1_xx_pos"))`, `r ci(x_("E1_xx_pos", "lo"), x_("E1_xx_pos", "hi"))`.

*Item by item.* In each of the `r e2[!is.na(diff), .N]` cells with at least 20 estimates both within and beyond one log unit of the true value (the 13 cells of @bahnik2021, the Cologne cathedral item and one of the two items of @yoon2021), the slope for far anchors was lower than the slope for near anchors (median difference `r f2(median(e2$diff, na.rm = TRUE))`). The other Yoon et al. item had too few near anchors for this analysis; the positive curvature reported below for the two Yoon et al. items together comes from a different specification (a quadratic fit to both items together, including the item not in this comparison).

*Standardised effect sizes.* Across cells, Hedges' *g* rose with extremity by `r f2(x_("E3_hedges_g_slope"))` per log unit, `r ci(x_("E3_hedges_g_slope", "lo"), x_("E3_hedges_g_slope", "hi"), 2)` ([@fig-across], panel B), in line with @roseler2022meta. The same cells therefore show a rising standardised effect and no detectable change in proportional pull.

*Extremity relative to response spread.* The across-cell extremity measure ignores how uncertain people are about each quantity. When we divided extremity by the spread of log estimates within each anchor condition (a measure that is itself affected by anchoring), the slope turned negative, *d* = `r f3(x_("E4_slope_on_scaled_extremity"))`, `r ci(x_("E4_slope_on_scaled_extremity", "lo"), x_("E4_slope_on_scaled_extremity", "hi"))`. When we instead entered extremity and spread as separate predictors, the extremity slope was `r f3(x_("E4_slope_adjusting_spread"))`, `r ci(x_("E4_slope_adjusting_spread", "lo"), x_("E4_slope_adjusting_spread", "hi"))`. The two specifications disagree, and a ratio predictor can produce spurious associations when its denominator is related to the outcome's precision, so this analysis does not settle whether the across-cell pattern reflects how anchors were placed relative to people's uncertainty.

*Relaxed calibration.* To check whether the model failures stem from the calibration to Jacowitz and Kahneman's index, we drew 300 parameter sets per model from wide ranges without calibration and simulated each on the OpAQ designs. None of these draws reproduced the observed *b*, *g*, *d* and mean index jointly (all four inside their observed 95% confidence intervals); with 300 draws per model, this shows that such parameter settings are rare, not that none exist. Within-item *b* and *g* together were reproduced by `r e5[model == "M4"]$within_b_and_g` of 300 M4 draws, `r e5[model == "M1R"]$within_b_and_g` M1R draws and `r e5[model == "M3"]$within_b_and_g` M3 draws, and by no M1 or M2 draw; the across-cell *d* and mean index together were reproduced by `r e5[model == "M2"]$across_d_and_ai` M2 draws, `r e5[model == "M1"]$across_d_and_ai` M1 draws and `r e5[model == "M1R"]$across_d_and_ai` M1R draws, and by no M3 or M4 draw.

*Constant weight on the raw scale.* M2 assumes a constant weight on the log scale. We also simulated a constant weight on the raw scale (the estimate is a weighted average of anchor and belief in raw units; weights drawn from .30 to .60; 300 replicates). Passed through the H1 estimator, this model predicted a negative pooled curvature, *g* = `r f3(e6_("g"))`, `r ci(e6_("g", "lo"), e6_("g", "hi"))`, an interval that contains the observed value, because on the log scale raw averaging flattens the response to anchors below the belief. It predicted opposite curvatures on the two sides of the true value, however: negative below (`r f3(e6_("g_below"))`, `r ci(e6_("g_below", "lo"), e6_("g_below", "hi"))`) and positive above (`r f3(e6_("g_above"))`, `r ci(e6_("g_above", "lo"), e6_("g_above", "hi"))`). The observed curvature above the true value was negative (`r f3(x_("E1_xx_pos"))`), which contradicts raw-scale constant weighting. The preregistered pooled test alone would not have ruled out this model.

*Study-specific estimates.* The curvature was negative in @bahnik2021, *g* = `r f3(rc_("R1c_g_Bahník, 2021a"))`, `r ci(rc_("R1c_g_Bahník, 2021a", "lo"), rc_("R1c_g_Bahník, 2021a", "hi"))`, and in the Cologne cathedral item of @imhoff2023, `r f3(rc_("R1c_g_Imhoff & Barker, 2022, Study 2"))`, `r ci(rc_("R1c_g_Imhoff & Barker, 2022, Study 2", "lo"), rc_("R1c_g_Imhoff & Barker, 2022, Study 2", "hi"))`; it was imprecise in Frech et al. (2021), `r f3(rc_("R1c_g_Frech et al., 2021"))`, `r ci(rc_("R1c_g_Frech et al., 2021", "lo"), rc_("R1c_g_Frech et al., 2021", "hi"), 2)`, and positive in the two items of @yoon2021, whose anchors were participants' own height or age, `r f3(rc_("R1c_g_Yoon et al., 2021, Form C"))`, `r ci(rc_("R1c_g_Yoon et al., 2021, Form C", "lo"), rc_("R1c_g_Yoon et al., 2021, Form C", "hi"))`. @imhoff2023 reported a linear relation between anchor and estimate for the Cologne cathedral item on the raw scale; a linear raw-scale relation also produces a declining log-scale elasticity for anchors below the belief, so this item alone does not discriminate between log-scale plausibility models and raw-scale averaging.

These analyses were added after a code review and were not preregistered.

*Calibration scale.* The preregistered calibration compared the models' log-scale anchoring index with Jacowitz and Kahneman's value of about .49, which they computed on the raw scale. Recalibrating every model to a raw-scale index accepted largely the same parameter values (`r paste(sprintf("%s: %d of %d", s1acc$model, s1acc$both, s1acc$log_scale), collapse = "; ")` of the originally accepted grid points were also accepted), and new predictions from the recalibrated models led to the same conclusion: only M1R survived the shape criteria.

Adding study-level random effects gave *g* = `r f3(s_("S2_study_random_effect"))`, `r ci(s_("S2_study_random_effect", "lo"), s_("S2_study_random_effect", "hi"))`. # Discussion

Within items, estimates responded less to changes in the anchor as the anchor moved away from the true value. Near the truth, the local elasticity was `r f2(P$b)`; for anchors a factor of 2.7 from the truth it was `r f2(loc_el(1))`, and for anchors a factor of 7.4 away, `r f2(loc_el(2))`. The decline appeared on both sides of the true value, in every item with enough near and far anchors, and in the one fixed-anchor item with many anchor levels. Across two-anchor studies, where authors chose one anchor pair per item, the anchoring index showed no detectable decline, and its point estimate leaned the other way.

## What the within-item result rules out

The negative curvature contradicts two simple implementations. Anchor-and-adjust with a fixed number of steps predicts that far anchors keep more of their distance, because a bounded number of bounded steps cannot correct a large gap; the data show the reverse. Constant-weight integration on the log scale predicts no change in proportional pull; it too is contradicted. Constant weighting on the raw scale predicts the observed pooled curvature, but also a rising elasticity above the true value, which the exploratory side-specific estimates contradict. The implementations that predict a decline on both sides share one feature: the anchor's influence is limited by how plausible it is. The within-item shape is consistent with this feature, but the calibrated versions of these models did not reproduce the data quantitatively, so plausibility-limited influence is one possible account rather than an established mechanism. This holds for adjustment that stops at the edge of the plausible range [@mussweiler2001; @epley2006] and for integration that discounts implausible anchors [@wegener2001; @turner2016]. The resource-rational variant can also produce a decline, but its calibrated versions did not reproduce the observed combination of elasticity and curvature. The result fits earlier experiments with few anchor levels in which implausible anchors had proportionally smaller effects [@chapman1994; @mussweiler2001; @wegener2001], the distance-decaying anchoring weight of @barrera2024, and the levelling-off of assimilation to symbolic anchors in dot estimation [@imhoff2023]. It extends these findings to general-knowledge magnitudes, to anchors far outside the plausible range, and to a proportional outcome. In a dot-estimation task with anchors 35% or 70% away from the true value, the more distant anchors produced larger estimation errors [@mayer2024]; a larger absolute effect is compatible with a declining proportional pull, so the two findings do not conflict.

Relative to the overall strength of anchoring, the decline was smaller than the calibrated versions of M3 and M4 predicted: their intervals for ρ lay below the observed value, and far anchors still had a positive slope. Far anchors thus pulled estimates more than a hard plausibility boundary or a steep plausibility discount allows, at least within the calibrated parameter ranges. A mixture in which the weight of an anchor falls gradually but does not vanish could describe this. The data do not identify such a model, and we did not test one.

## The across-cell pattern

The across-cell analysis did not reproduce the within-item decline, and no model with a single parameter set reproduced both patterns. Two explanations are plausible, and our data cannot fully separate them. First, extremity measured against the true value is not extremity measured against people's uncertainty. Researchers may place anchors further from the truth for quantities that people know poorly. An anchor ten times the true population of a city may be less implausible than an anchor twice the height of a familiar building. When we scaled extremity by the spread of estimates, the across-cell slope turned negative, as the within-item analysis and the plausibility accounts predict, but entering spread as a separate predictor left the extremity slope positive and imprecise. Because the spread is itself affected by anchoring, neither analysis resolves the question. Second, the two sets differ in anchor type: the within-item set is mostly random anchors, and the across-cell set only fixed or relevant anchors. The models make the same shape predictions for both, but it is possible that informative anchors lose less pull with extremity than anchors people know to be random. The fixed-anchor stratum of the within-item set pointed in the same direction as the random-anchor stratum but was too small for the preregistered test, and only one fixed-anchor item had enough anchor levels to show the decline on its own.

The divergence also bears on how moderator analyses of anchoring should be read. In the same cells, the standardised effect rose with extremity while the proportional index did not change detectably. Meta-analytic findings that larger anchor distances produce larger standardised effects [@roseler2022meta] therefore say little about whether extreme anchors are more influential per unit of distance. Tests of anchoring theories need a proportional outcome and variation in extremity that the researcher controls.

## Limitations

The primary evidence rests largely on one study. Thirteen of the 20 within-item cells, and `r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * wct[study == "Bahník, 2021a", sum(estimates)] / P$n_rows)` of the within-item estimates, come from @bahnik2021, in which participants compared 13 random anchors with 13 different lengths and heights. Without this study the within-item curvature had the same sign but a confidence interval too wide to be informative. The random anchors also differ from the fixed anchors that dominate applied settings. The preregistered test of the fixed-anchor stratum was not informative; in an exploratory analysis, the one fixed-anchor item with 20 anchor levels showed the same decline, but it is a single item. A direct test of the extremity function for informative anchors needs experiments that present many anchor levels for many items.

Second, extremity was measured relative to the true value, not relative to each participant's belief. Where people systematically over- or underestimate a quantity, the anchor's distance from their belief differs from its distance from the truth. The simulations included item-level bias to account for this, and the curvature was negative on both sides of the true value. However, a study that elicits unanchored estimates or plausible ranges from the same participants would give a cleaner measure.

Third, the models were specified on the log scale and calibrated to a single external benchmark. The shape predictions of M1, M2, M3 and M4 follow from their structure and held across all calibrated parameter values, but the level predictions depend on the calibration, and the resource-rational model's predictions depend strongly on its time cost and on how uncertain people are. That this model survived our tests reflects the width of its predictions more than a close fit. Formal tests of resource-rational anchoring need independent measures of the time cost and of people's uncertainty.

Fourth, OpAQ harmonises data from many studies, and its codes do not always match the original designs: the two items of @yoon2021 used participants' own height or age as anchors, and the anchors of the Cologne cathedral item were described by its authors as random. Harmonisation can also introduce errors. We found one item whose responses were recorded in different units from its anchors and true value, and an unpublished 2026 corrigendum, posted on the OpAQ project page for a related publication by the same group, suggests that the item coding of another study (Weber et al., 2021) may contain errors. Our rules removed the first; excluding the second made the across-cell slope positive and significant. We used only positive ratio-scale quantities with open response scales, so the results do not speak to dates, percentages, bounded scales or preferences.

## Conclusion

Within the same questions, estimates responded less to changes in the anchor when the anchor was far from the true value than when it was close to it. The evidence comes mostly from random anchors for lengths and heights in one study, with the same pattern in the one fixed-anchor item that had many anchor levels. It contradicts anchor-and-adjust with a fixed number of steps and constant-weight integration, and is consistent with accounts in which an anchor's influence is limited by its plausibility. No calibrated model, however, explained the combined results: the plausibility models predicted a steeper within-item decline and a falling across-cell trend. Across studies with researcher-chosen anchors, the pattern was not visible. Whether deliberately chosen, informative anchors, such as opening offers in negotiations, also show diminishing returns to extremity cannot be answered with these data. The extremity function should be estimated within items, with proportional measures and with anchors of the kind used in practice.
